ocar.opportunity: A complete chordate larval connectome, together with invariant cell lineages, lets motor circuits be studied cell by cell in a vertebrate sister group.
ocar.challenge: Tunicate larvae have only a brief window to swim and settle, and it has been unclear how their small Motor Ganglion relates to vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.
ocar.action: Piekarz and Stolfi, in Journal of Experimental Zoology B (catalog year 2023; published form 2024), review development, connectivity, function, and identities of Motor Ganglion neurons, drawing mostly on Ciona.
ocar.resolution: They treat the Motor Ganglion, formerly called visceral or trunk ganglion, as a putative rhombospinal homolog at the base of the tail. In Ciona intestinalis the larval CNS has 177 neurons plus about 50 peripheral sensory cells; the Motor Ganglion core is a network of 7–8 bilateral pairs. The review argues that this cellular simplicity plus the first complete chordate connectome makes the ganglion a model for how chordate central pattern generators are assembled.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion asks how those CPGs generate rhythmic swimming and how the circuits are set up within a chordate developmental program; the article reports no original data.

summaries.beginner: A sea-squirt larva swims with a tiny cluster of motor neurons at the base of its tail. This review explains how that cluster develops and is wired, and why it may be a miniature version of the vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.
summaries.intermediate: Piekarz and Stolfi (Journal of Experimental Zoology B; catalog 2023, published 2024) review the tunicate larval Motor Ganglion, mainly in Ciona. They place tunicates as the vertebrate sister group and cite a Ciona CNS of 177 neurons plus about 50 peripheral sensory cells, with a Motor Ganglion core of 7–8 bilateral pairs that control swimming. Molecular and functional comparisons are used to argue for homology with vertebrate hindbrain and/or spinal cord (a “rhombospinal” region). The piece is a review of existing lineage, physiology, and connectome work, not a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: PMC copy is an author manuscript of a review; the data-availability statement says there are no original data. Neuron counts (177 CNS, ~50 peripheral, 7–8 MG pairs) are those stated in the extract and should be checked against Ryan et al. reconstructions. Catalog year is 2023; the published form is dated May 2024.

plain_language_summary: A sea-squirt larva swims with a tiny cluster of motor neurons at the base of its tail. This review explains how that cluster develops and is wired, and why it may be a miniature version of the vertebrate hindbrain and spinal cord.

ocar.opportunity: Asynchronous insect flight is used by more than 600,000 species, yet the central-pattern-generating circuit that times wing power has been hard to pin down in a miniaturized nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Electrical synapses are classically expected to synchronize coupled neurons, which would not produce the staggered motoneuron firing needed for stable wingbeat power.
ocar.action: Hürkey, Niemeyer, Schleimer, Ryglewski, Schreiber, and Duch, in Nature (2023), combine electrophysiology, optophysiology, Drosophila genetics, and mathematical modelling of the five identified dorsal-longitudinal motoneurons (MN1–5).
ocar.resolution: The CPG is those motoneurons linked by electrical synapses that, contrary to doctrine, splay activity in time rather than synchronizing it. Weak gap junctions plus neuron-intrinsic excitability (including Shab delayed-rectifier current) can desynchronize small networks and convert unpatterned premotor input into a fixed activation sequence. The authors report the mechanism as conserved across multiple species and argue that connectomics must detect electrical synapses, not only chemical ones.
ocar.future_work: The paper frames a wider versatility of electrical synapses in circuit dynamics; how generally the desynchronizing regime applies beyond flight motoneurons is left as an implication rather than a mapped inventory.

summaries.beginner: Flies beat their wings with a tiny motor circuit. This Nature paper shows that the electrical synapses in that circuit do not lock the cells together; they stagger them, which helps keep flight stable.
summaries.intermediate: Hürkey, Niemeyer, Schleimer, Ryglewski, Schreiber, and Duch (Nature, 2023) study the Drosophila asynchronous-flight CPG formed by motoneurons MN1–5 of the dorsal longitudinal muscle. Using electrophysiology, optophysiology, genetics, and modelling, they find that electrical synapses among these motoneurons desynchronize rather than synchronize firing. Weak coupling plus specific excitability dynamics, including Shab potassium current, produce stereotyped sequences that stabilize wingbeat power. The authors present this as a generic small-network mechanism conserved across several insect species and as a reason to score gap junctions in connectomes.
summaries.advanced: Open-access Nature article. Extended-data numbers in the extract (Shab ~50% of delayed-rectifier current in MN1–5; RNAi and overexpression replicate counts) are from figure legends, not a single summary statistic for the whole CPG. ‘More than 600,000 species’ is the paper’s stated scope for asynchronous flight. Chemical-synapse maps alone would miss the coupling they study.

plain_language_summary: Flies beat their wings with a tiny motor circuit. This Nature paper shows that the electrical synapses in that circuit do not lock the cells together; they stagger them, which helps keep flight stable.

ocar.opportunity: Hunger and thirst compete, so a wiring diagram of how internal state is turned into ingestion choices can show how animals prioritize nutrients.
ocar.challenge: Food and water circuits are often studied separately, leaving the downstream path from shared interoceptive neurons unclear.
ocar.action: González-Segarra, Pontes, Jourjine, Del Toro, and Scott, in a June 2023 bioRxiv preprint, use the fly brain connectome plus in vivo manipulations to trace partners of the four Interoceptive Subesophageal zone Neurons (ISNs).
ocar.resolution: ISNs synapse onto a Bilateral T-shaped neuron (BiT) that projects to neuroendocrine centers and, like the ISNs, oppositely regulates sugar versus water ingestion. Downstream peptide cells include insulin-producing cells and CCAP neurons (both bidirectional for sugar versus water) and CCHa2R-RA neurons (water only). The authors conclude that the ingestive decision is implemented by a broad peptidergic network that integrates nutritional state.
ocar.future_work: How this network generalizes beyond the assayed peptides and how it maps onto mammalian hunger–thirst interactions are framed as comparative implications of a preprint.

summaries.beginner: Flies decide whether to drink sugar or water using a few brain cells that sense hunger and thirst. This preprint follows those cells into a hormone-releasing network that pushes the two choices in opposite directions.
summaries.intermediate: González-Segarra and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2023) start from four Drosophila Interoceptive Subesophageal zone Neurons that oppositely control sucrose and water ingestion. Using the fly brain connectome they identify a postsynaptic Bilateral T-shaped neuron (BiT) projecting to neuroendocrine centers; in vivo manipulations show BiT also oppositely regulates sugar and water. Downstream partners include insulin-producing cells, crustacean cardioactive peptide neurons, and CCHa2R-RA neurons, which contribute differentially to the two ingestive programs. The paper treats connectome partners as a hypothesis generator then tests them physiologically.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint (version posted 22 June 2023). Circuit claims in the extract are qualitative; figure legends report n and p-values for specific optogenetic assays but not a single network-wide synapse count. ‘Novel cell type’ BiT is the authors’ designation from connectome matching.

plain_language_summary: Flies decide whether to drink sugar or water using a few brain cells that sense hunger and thirst. This preprint follows those cells into a hormone-releasing network that pushes the two choices in opposite directions.

ocar.opportunity: If synaptic links could be recovered from calcium time series, functional recordings could be turned into wiring hypotheses even where electron microscopy is unavailable.
ocar.challenge: Real recordings are short, noisy, sparsely sampled, and often miss nodes, so link scores may not split cleanly into true edges versus non-edges.
ocar.action: Banerjee, Chandra, and Ott, in a PNAS inaugural article (2023), compare Granger causality, transfer entropy, and a reservoir-computer method on Lorenz-oscillator networks and on C. elegans neuronal calcium data with known ground-truth connectivity, and they test surrogate data for confidence.
ocar.resolution: On synthetic data the reservoir method improves with shorter sampling interval, longer duration, fuller node coverage, and lower noise. On C. elegans, limitations prevent clean two-group score separation; the authors argue that failure of scores to bimodally separate is itself a diagnostic, and that related simulated networks can be used as confidence-building tests when the true graph is unknown.
ocar.future_work: They present the worm tests as especially relevant to other calcium-imaged systems such as Drosophila and zebrafish, not as a finished inference of the hermaphrodite connectome from calcium alone.

summaries.beginner: Can you guess which neurons are wired together just from how their calcium signals wiggle? This paper tests three guessing methods on worm data and on toy chaotic networks, and shows why messy, short recordings make the job hard.
summaries.intermediate: Banerjee, Chandra, and Ott (PNAS, 2023) score directed links with Granger causality, transfer entropy, and reservoir computing. They systematically degrade Lorenz-network time series (sampling interval, duration, noise, partial nodes) and apply the same tools to C. elegans calcium fluorescence with known synaptic ground truth. Reservoir inference on the synthetic data tracks experimental quality; C. elegans scores do not cleanly separate links from non-links. Surrogate data are assessed as a route to statistical confidence when ground truth is unavailable.
summaries.advanced: Inaugural NAS article. The extract does not report a single accuracy number for C. elegans inference. Ground-truth comparison is to the known synaptic network; electrical synapses and neuromodulation are not the scoring target. ‘Ideal’ versus ‘non-ideal’ score distributions are qualitative in the discussion.

plain_language_summary: Can you guess which neurons are wired together just from how their calcium signals wiggle? This paper tests three guessing methods on worm data and on toy chaotic networks, and shows why messy, short recordings make the job hard.

ocar.opportunity: Human stem-cell retinal neurons will only restore vision if they can form new synapses after they are taken out of organoids and placed in a new environment.
ocar.challenge: Intact organoids show calcium signs of synapses, but direct evidence that dissociated cells reconnect had been lacking, and animal xenografts are limited by species differences in synaptic machinery.
ocar.action: Ludwig, Mayerl, Gao, Banghart, Bacig, Fernandez Zepeda, Zhao, and Gamm, in PNAS (2023), apply rabies-virus monosynaptic retrograde tracing to dissociated early human pluripotent stem-cell retinal organoid cultures, with a high-throughput labeling and counting pipeline.
ocar.resolution: Dissociated organoid neurons form de novo connections. Photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells are the two largest traced presynaptic populations among cell types of therapeutic interest. Tracing demonstrates connectivity plasticity, not mature ribbon-synapse physiology; the authors used a pre-ribbon stage and pseudotyped virus to avoid a known barrier to rabies spread at adult ribbons.
ocar.future_work: They position the assay as a complement to animal grafting and as a platform for future work on later-stage photoreceptors and on enhancing synaptogenesis for cell replacement.

summaries.beginner: Lab-grown human retinal cells only help if they can plug back into a circuit. This study uses a tracing virus to show that after the cells are pulled apart, photoreceptors and ganglion cells do form new synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Ludwig and colleagues (PNAS, 2023) dissociate early human pluripotent stem-cell retinal organoids and use glycoprotein-deleted rabies monosynaptic tracing to detect new connections. Photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells dominate the traced presynaptic pool. The authors stress that tracing is not a direct measure of synaptic maturity or function, and that they assayed stages before ribbon-synapse formation. They present the method as an in vitro complement to preclinical transplantation, where human–host synaptic incompatibility is a concern.
summaries.advanced: Open-access PNAS research article. The extract does not give a single reconnection rate. Catalog organism tags include mouse retina datasets; the paper itself is human organoid culture. Ribbon-synapse caveats are the authors’.

plain_language_summary: Lab-grown human retinal cells only help if they can plug back into a circuit. This study uses a tracing virus to show that after the cells are pulled apart, photoreceptors and ganglion cells do form new synapses.

ocar.opportunity: A cell-type-resolved wiring diagram of the mouse claustrum would let its proposed roles in attention and cortex-wide coordination be tested at cellular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Claustrum borders in mouse are disputed, and bulk tracing mixes cell types and can contaminate neighboring insular cortex.
ocar.action: Wang, Wang, Kuo, Xie, Kuang, Hirokawa, and colleagues at the Allen Institute, in Cell Reports (2023), combine multimodal references with bulk anterograde/retrograde viral tracing and single-neuron reconstructions registered to CCFv3.
ocar.resolution: They delineate the claustrum as one neuronal group embedded in agranular insular cortex. Prefrontal cortex supplies more projecting cell types than other cortical modules, with layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons predominating. Nine morphological types of claustrum principal neurons innervate functionally linked cortical targets, preferring midline cortex, secondary motor area, and entorhinal cortex.
ocar.future_work: Limitations they list include rabies TVA leak, incomplete transsynaptic coverage, injection-site contamination, registration error, and axons of passage inflating anterograde terminal fields; they urge cross-checks with anterograde, single-cell, and BARseq data.

summaries.beginner: The claustrum is a thin sheet of cells tucked beside cortex and wired to much of the brain. This mouse map shows which cortical cell types talk to it and how its own cells send axons back to matching sets of areas.
summaries.intermediate: Wang et al. (Cell Reports, 2023) use Allen Institute multimodal atlases, bulk anterograde and retrograde viruses, and single-neuron tracing to map mouse claustrum. They treat CLA as a single group embedded in agranular insula. Inputs are biased toward prefrontal modules, especially layer 5 IT cells. Outputs comprise nine morphological principal-cell types with topographic innervation of functionally related cortex, especially midline, MOs, and entorhinal targets. The discussion catalogs viral-tracing and registration artifacts rather than claiming a complete EM connectome.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript. ‘Nine morphological types’ and the prefrontal/L5-IT bias are stated in the summary; the extract does not list per-type synapse counts. This is mesoscale viral tracing plus light-level single-cell morphology, not synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: The claustrum is a thin sheet of cells tucked beside cortex and wired to much of the brain. This mouse map shows which cortical cell types talk to it and how its own cells send axons back to matching sets of areas.

ocar.opportunity: After spinal injury, recovery depends on which brain-to-cord pathways survive, not only on the famous corticospinal tract.
ocar.challenge: Most studies profile a handful of motor command populations and ignore dozens of autonomic and modulatory supraspinal groups.
ocar.action: Wang, Romanski, Mehra, Wang, Brannigan, Campbell, Petsko, Tsoulfas, and Blackmore, in eLife (2022), combine optimized retrograde viral labeling, 3D imaging, and atlas registration in adult mice, and release a web resource.
ocar.resolution: Tens of thousands of supraspinal neurons are assigned to 69 identified regions. The workflow is used to map topographic brain-to-spinal-level relationships, population-specific injury sensitivity, and links between spared regional neurons and variable functional recovery. Nuclear-localized fluorophores and confocal 3D imaging yield higher dual-innervation estimates than some prior reports (examples in the discussion: 8% in cerebellospinal versus prior complete segregation; over 50% in corticospinal versus almost none; more than 40% in gigantocellular versus about 20%).
ocar.future_work: They argue that regenerative and clinical work should include understudied autonomic and postural populations, and they note that dual-innervation rates depend strongly on detection threshold.

summaries.beginner: Many brain regions send axons into the spinal cord, not just the famous motor pathway. This mouse study labels those cells brain-wide after injury and asks which leftover groups go with better recovery.
summaries.intermediate: Wang, Romanski, Mehra, and colleagues (eLife, 2022) profile the adult-mouse supraspinal mesoconnectome with retrograde AAV, 3D imaging, and digital-atlas registration, assigning tens of thousands of neurons to 69 regions and posting a web resource. They apply the pipeline to spinal-level topography, injury sensitivity, and recovery correlates. Discussion of dual cervical–lumbar innervation stresses detection thresholds: brighter nuclear labels and confocal imaging raise dual-label rates relative to earlier light-sheet or less sensitive studies. Editors highlight tissue clearing and viral labeling for spinal-injury research.
summaries.advanced: Open-access eLife. ‘Tens of thousands’ and 69 regions are the paper’s stated yield; the extract does not give a single grand total of labeled cells. Dual-innervation percentages are the authors’ estimates versus cited priors, not independent reanalysis here. Mesoscale soma counts, not synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: Many brain regions send axons into the spinal cord, not just the famous motor pathway. This mouse study labels those cells brain-wide after injury and asks which leftover groups go with better recovery.

ocar.opportunity: If brain-wide dynamics sit near criticality, comparing a modular human connectome with a denser fly map can show which graph features create an extended critical regime.
ocar.challenge: Prior human-connectome simulations suggested Griffiths-phase (subcritical, rare-region) criticality driven by heterogeneity; it was unknown whether the fruit-fly central-brain graph would behave the same.
ocar.action: Ódor, Deco, and Kelling, in Physical Review Research (2022), run the Kuramoto synchronization model on the 21,662-node fruit-fly connectome and compare the transition with the KKI-18 human connectome and with random graphs.
ocar.resolution: They describe the fly graph as less heterogeneous, lacking modular structure, and high in topological dimension. Its synchronization transition is mean-field-like: the transition region is wider than in random graphs but much narrower than for KKI-18. They attribute the difference to modularity and dimension.
ocar.future_work: The introduction notes that such numerics do not prove whole-brain criticality and remain inside model assumptions; the fly result is offered as a basis for understanding human critical dynamics, not as a neural recording study.

summaries.beginner: Some theories say brains hover near a tipping point between quiet and fully locked-together activity. This physics paper compares a fly wiring diagram with a human one and finds the fly’s tipping point is sharper.
summaries.intermediate: Ódor, Deco, and Kelling (Physical Review Research, 2022; arXiv title prepends “What makes us humans”) simulate Kuramoto oscillators on a 21,662-node fruit-fly connectome (hemibrain-scale resource cited in the bibliography). Relative to prior KKI-18 human-connectome work, they find a mean-field-like synchronization transition whose width exceeds random graphs but is much smaller than the human case, which they link to weaker modularity and higher topological dimension in the fly graph.
summaries.advanced: Same paper as the catalog record; the PDF title adds a popular prefix. Node count 21,662 is the authors’. This is a dynamical simulation on an anatomical graph, not new EM or physiology. Criticality claims are model-dependent, as the authors state.

plain_language_summary: Some theories say brains hover near a tipping point between quiet and fully locked-together activity. This physics paper compares a fly wiring diagram with a human one and finds the fly’s tipping point is sharper.

ocar.opportunity: Balanced cortical networks are a standard explanation of low, irregular, weakly correlated spiking; a theory that allows realistic connection symmetry could show extra dynamical phases cortex might use for computation.
ocar.challenge: Classic balanced-network theory assumes uncorrelated random connectivity, whereas local cortical wiring includes reciprocal and other symmetric structure.
ocar.action: Berlemont and Mongillo, in a March 2022 bioRxiv preprint, develop a mean-field theory for balanced rate networks whose synapses have an arbitrary symmetry level, find the fixed point, and locate its stability boundary.
ocar.resolution: Above a critical synaptic gain that depends on symmetry, and for positive symmetry, they report a previously unreported phase: many marginally stable fixed points, non-exponential relaxation, and broken ergodicity—a glassy phase. They discuss it as a candidate for cortical dynamical and computational regimes.
ocar.future_work: Relevance to cortex is proposed rather than fit to a particular dataset; Dale’s-law constraints and full spiking networks are noted as theoretical context in the notes.

summaries.beginner: Brain models often assume random wiring that keeps excitation and inhibition in a tight tug-of-war. This theory paper shows that when connections are a bit symmetric, the network can freeze into a glassy landscape of many almost-stable states.
summaries.intermediate: Berlemont and Mongillo (bioRxiv, 2022) give a mean-field theory for balanced rate networks with tunable synaptic symmetry (log-normal efficacies; threshold-linear transfer). They locate the balanced fixed point and a symmetry-dependent critical gain. For positive symmetry beyond that gain they describe a glassy phase dominated by marginally stable fixed points, slow relaxation, and broken ergodicity. The extract presents equations and the phase claim; it does not fit in vivo spike statistics quantitatively.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. ‘Previously unreported phase’ is the authors’ claim. No connectomic reconstruction is performed. Cortical interpretation is conceptual.

plain_language_summary: Brain models often assume random wiring that keeps excitation and inhibition in a tight tug-of-war. This theory paper shows that when connections are a bit symmetric, the network can freeze into a glassy landscape of many almost-stable states.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic tracing of neurons from 3D light-microscope volumes is needed for morphology and connectomics, but voxel segmentation plus tracing is memory-heavy and sensitive to gaps and background.
ocar.challenge: Convolutional segmentation followed by tracing inherits image noise and disconnected arbors; dense voxels spend compute on empty background.
ocar.action: Zhao, Wang, Zhang, and Cai, in WACV (catalog year 2022; arXiv 2022), introduce PointNeuron: point-cloud graph convolutional networks that predict skeleton points and then their connectivity, writing SWC files, evaluated on the Janelia-Fly subset of BigNeuron.
ocar.resolution: They report competitive reconstruction versus voxel deep-learning baselines, fewer false-positive branches than APP2 in visualizations, about 95.6% lower input memory by dropping background voxels, and a proposed-model F1 of 71.7±17.48 in their ablation table. They suggest the geometry/topology approach may transfer to other 3D medical surfaces.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion positions the method as a pipeline for automatic reconstruction rather than a completed fly-brain connectome.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure traces usually means slicing a huge 3D grid. This computer-vision paper treats the neuron as a cloud of points instead, which is lighter and can follow thin branches through gaps.
summaries.intermediate: Zhao, Wang, Zhang, and Cai (WACV / arXiv, 2022) convert 3D neuron image volumes to point clouds, then use one GCN to predict skeleton points and another to predict their links, exporting SWC. On Janelia-Fly (BigNeuron) they report competitive accuracy, reduced false-positive arbors relative to APP2, and a large memory cut versus voxel networks (95.6% less input memory in the extract). Ablations compare loss terms, PointNet++, DGCNN, and downsampling; the proposed setting lists F1 71.7±17.48.
summaries.advanced: Conference/arXiv methods paper, not a biological reconstruction of a whole fly brain. Metrics are on BigNeuron Janelia-Fly; they should be read from the tables, not treated as a universal tracing accuracy. Code link is given as GitHub PointNeuron.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure traces usually means slicing a huge 3D grid. This computer-vision paper treats the neuron as a cloud of points instead, which is lighter and can follow thin branches through gaps.

ocar.opportunity: Human brain organoids contain 3D circuits, but conventional light microscopy cannot jointly capture whole-organoid layout and synaptic-scale contacts.
ocar.challenge: Organoids are millimeter-scale and opaque; high-NA optics have short working distance, and slicing destroys 3D context.
ocar.action: Rodriguez-Gatica, Iefremova, Sokhranyaeva, Yeung, Breitkreuz, Brüstle, Schwarz, and Kubitscheck, in a December 2021 bioRxiv preprint, combine tissue expansion with light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFEM), using CHAPS permeabilization to preserve fluorescent proteins.
ocar.resolution: Expansion of about 1.5- to 4-fold lets them move in one session from mesoscopic views to super-resolution, including mitotic cleavage planes and aligned pre- and postsynaptic proteins. They report imaging organoids up to 15 mm after preparation, following labeled cells for up to 14 months of culture, and effective resolutions they cite as laterally under 100 nm and axially down to 300 nm after 4× expansion. They note batch-to-batch developmental variability and that a 1 mm³ organoid expanded 4× imaged at that sampling would be an enormous (they estimate 340 TB) dataset.
ocar.future_work: They expect LSFEM to support developmental and disease studies; full-organoid synaptic maps at Nyquist sampling remain data-limited.

summaries.beginner: Mini-brains grown from stem cells are too big and cloudy for ordinary microscopes to see both the whole lump and single synapses. This preprint swells the tissue and uses a light-sheet microscope to zoom from the whole organoid down toward synaptic scale.
summaries.intermediate: Rodriguez-Gatica and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2021) combine expansion microscopy with light-sheet imaging of human brain organoids (LSFEM). CHAPS-based clearing/expansion (about 1.5–4×) preserves autofluorescent proteins and antibody stains in large samples (they cite up to 15 mm). They illustrate cleavage-plane geometry and pre/postsynaptic alignment, and they discuss previously reported effective resolutions after 4× expansion (laterally <100 nm, axially ~300 nm). Culture periods up to 14 months and strong batch variability are noted. A back-of-the-envelope 340 TB figure illustrates why whole-organoid Nyquist volumes are impractical.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. Expansion factors and resolution figures are those stated in the extract. 340 TB is an illustrative calculation, not a dataset they acquired. Not an EM connectome.

plain_language_summary: Mini-brains grown from stem cells are too big and cloudy for ordinary microscopes to see both the whole lump and single synapses. This preprint swells the tissue and uses a light-sheet microscope to zoom from the whole organoid down toward synaptic scale.

ocar.opportunity: Higher-order thalamus is a candidate hub for mixing cortical messages on a cortico-thalamo-cortical route, but whether single relay cells actually receive drivers from different cortical areas was untested at synapse resolution.
ocar.challenge: Light-level tracing cannot prove that sensory and motor layer-5 terminals converge on the same thalamic neuron.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri, in PNAS (2021), dual-label layer 5 of mouse S1 and M1 with ascorbate peroxidase in Rbp4-cre mice and reconstruct synapses in posterior medial nucleus (POm) with serial EM.
ocar.resolution: Nineteen of 33 reconstructed POm cells received convergent S1 and M1 layer-5 input. As a population, labeled layer-5 synapses were larger and more proximal on dendrites than unlabeled synapses. The authors conclude that many of these thalamic neurons integrate disparate cortical signals rather than relaying a single source.
ocar.future_work: They note incomplete labeling and incomplete dendritic reconstructions, so true convergence rates would likely be higher, and they treat driver status of M1→POm as less established than S1→POm.

summaries.beginner: Messages from touch cortex and movement cortex were thought to stay on separate lines through the thalamus. This electron-microscope study finds that many thalamic cells in the mouse actually collect both.
summaries.intermediate: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri (PNAS, 2021) combine genetic/viral peroxidase labeling of layer 5 in mouse somatosensory and motor cortex with serial EM in POm. Nineteen of 33 reconstructed relay cells receive both labeled input classes; layer-5 terminals are larger and more proximal than unlabeled synapses. They interpret this as integration in a transthalamic corticocortical path, contrasting with a pure-relay view modeled on LGN. Driver/modulator language is presented as a useful but partly hypothetical framework.
summaries.advanced: Convergence fraction 19/33 is from partial reconstructions and partial labeling; the authors say it is a lower bound. M1 driver identity is explicitly less certain than S1. ‘Connectomics’ here is targeted EM, not a whole-thalamus volume.

plain_language_summary: Messages from touch cortex and movement cortex were thought to stay on separate lines through the thalamus. This electron-microscope study finds that many thalamic cells in the mouse actually collect both.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mouse-brain light-microscopy volumes at submicron resolution are petabytes; cataloging somata, dendrites, full axons, and candidate synapses from them needs software that can share and proofread at that scale.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic-scale resolution and whole-brain axonal arbors cannot be handled by naive local reconstruction workflows.
ocar.action: Jiang, Wang, Liu, Zhao, Chen, Zhao, Xie, Ding, Ruan, Dong, Ascoli, Hawrylycz, Zeng, and Peng describe MorphoHub (Research Square preprint of a Neuroinformatics 2022 article): multi-level data and workflow management applied to 62 whole mouse brains.
ocar.resolution: They report 50,233 identified somata, dendritic profiles of 11,322 neurons, full dendrite-plus-axon reconstructions of 1,050 neurons, and 1.9 million putative synaptic sites from axonal boutons. Analysis and simulation of those data are presented as showing the approach’s promise for large-scale morphometry. Images are pointed to BICCN’s Brain Image Library; morphometry to a Vaa3D GitHub release.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion is that the computing framework meets anatomic workflow needs for very large morphometry; it is not a claim of a complete synaptic mouse connectome.

summaries.beginner: A mouse brain imaged in fine 3D detail fills petabytes. This platform helps teams mark cell bodies, trace dendrites and long axons, and flag likely synapses across dozens of whole brains.
summaries.intermediate: Jiang et al. (Neuroinformatics 2022; extract is the January 2021 Research Square preprint) present MorphoHub for petabyte whole-brain morphometry. On 62 mouse brains they report 50,233 somata, dendrites of 11,322 neurons, complete 3-D reconstructions of 1,050 neurons, and 1.9 million bouton-derived putative synapses. The pipeline emphasizes remote collaborative proofreading (TeraVR is mentioned in author contributions). Putative synapses are light-microscopic bouton detections, not EM-verified contacts.
summaries.advanced: Counts are those stated in the preprint abstract. Catalog year is 2021; version of record is Neuroinformatics 19 February 2022. ‘Potential synaptic morphometry’ is bouton-based and should not be equated with EM synapses.

plain_language_summary: A mouse brain imaged in fine 3D detail fills petabytes. This platform helps teams mark cell bodies, trace dendrites and long axons, and flag likely synapses across dozens of whole brains.

ocar.opportunity: Animals adapt reaches within minutes, and motor-cortex activity changes with them; knowing whether those changes come from local rewiring or from altered inputs would constrain what a connectome can explain about rapid learning.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic weights cannot be measured densely in vivo during adaptation, and preserved neural covariance has been taken as evidence against local connectivity change.
ocar.action: Feulner, Perich, Chowdhury, Miller, Gallego, and Clopath, in Nature Communications (2022), train a modular recurrent network (PMd- and M1-like modules) on visuomotor perturbation tasks, comparing plasticity in inputs (Hinput) versus local recurrent weights (Hlocal).
ocar.resolution: Hinput yields small activity changes and largely preserved covariance, as expected. Hlocal needs only small, correlated weight changes and produces activity and covariance shifts still within experimental range. Larger behavioral remapping (a target–reach reassociation) separates the two. Experimental patterns—larger activity change in PMd than M1—better match Hinput, supporting plasticity upstream of motor cortices for rapid visuomotor adaptation.
ocar.future_work: They suggest designing tasks with bigger behavioral change to distinguish the hypotheses empirically; the model does not measure synapses in animals.

summaries.beginner: When you quickly adjust a reaching movement, motor-cortex activity shifts. This modelling paper asks whether that means the local wires changed, and finds that small, structured weight tweaks—or changes in incoming signals—can both look a lot like the recordings.
summaries.intermediate: Feulner et al. (Nature Communications, 2022) use a modular RNN as a qualitative stand-in for primate motor cortex during visuomotor rotation. Learning via input weights (Hinput) preserves covariance; learning via local connectivity (Hlocal) also stays within recorded activity and covariance ranges because successful adaptation uses small, low-dimensional, correlated weight updates. A reassociation task splits the hypotheses more clearly. Matching to data (larger PMd than M1 activity change) favors Hinput for rapid VR adaptation, unlike multi-day skill learning where M1 rewiring is reported.
summaries.advanced: Simulation study; no new connectome or synaptic physiology. ‘Within the range of experimental recordings’ is the authors’ qualitative comparison. Covariance preservation is not proof of frozen synapses.

plain_language_summary: When you quickly adjust a reaching movement, motor-cortex activity shifts. This modelling paper asks whether that means the local wires changed, and finds that small, structured weight tweaks—or changes in incoming signals—can both look a lot like the recordings.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstructions show precise partner choice in dense neuropil; the molecules that implement that choice are the complementary explanation of how those graphs form.
ocar.challenge: Many adhesion systems look similar at the domain level yet act at different times and places, so a single ‘synaptic recognition code’ is easy to oversimplify.
ocar.action: Chowdhury, Watters, and Biederer, in Current Topics in Developmental Biology (2021), review vertebrate synaptic recognition molecules along a developmental sequence: initial wiring, rejection of wrong partners, synapse specification, and removal of inappropriate synapses.
ocar.resolution: They survey cadherins, immunoglobulin-superfamily proteins, Semaphorins/Plexins, leucine-rich-repeat proteins, and neurexins with their binders, plus secreted factors. Recurring themes are cell-type-specific expression, combinatorial action, alternative splicing, and post-translational modification. Laminated structures such as hippocampus and retina are highlighted as advantageous assays; proteomics and single-cell expression are noted as methodological advances. A closing section links aberrant recognition to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disease.
ocar.future_work: The outlook calls for deeper accounts of how these systems yield the precision and diversity of connections; the chapter is a review, not a new screen.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams show which neurons touch, but not which molecular nametags told them to. This book chapter reviews the sticky and repulsive proteins that help vertebrate neurons pick, reject, specify, and later prune synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Chowdhury, Watters, and Biederer (Curr. Top. Dev. Biol., 2021) review adhesion, signaling, and secreted recognition molecules in vertebrate synaptogenesis. Organization is developmental: targeting, mismatch rejection, specification, and synapse elimination. Major families include cadherins, IgSF, Semaphorin/Plexin, LRR proteins, and neurexin complexes. They emphasize combinatorial codes, splicing, and PTMs, and they discuss disease relevance. Connectomic reconstructions (Kasthuri et al.; Motta et al.) are cited as revealing the anatomical patterns these molecules must explain.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a review chapter. No new quantitative connectome. Disease links are discussed at the level of the review, not a clinical trial.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams show which neurons touch, but not which molecular nametags told them to. This book chapter reviews the sticky and repulsive proteins that help vertebrate neurons pick, reject, specify, and later prune synapses.

ocar.opportunity: A connectional map of adult zebrafish pallial zones would show whether this everted cortex is a set of dedicated modules or a highly mixed network.
ocar.challenge: Pallial areas are distinguished by topography, cytoarchitecture, immunohistochemistry, and genes, but their mutual and extrapallial connections were incompletely surveyed.
ocar.action: Yáñez, Folgueira, Lamas, and Anadón, in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, use carbocyanine tracing and ancillary anatomy on the adult zebrafish dorsal telencephalon.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports poor interconnectivity among major pallial zones, especially between medial (Dm), lateral/dorsal (Dl, Dd), and posterior (Dp) regions, suggesting dedicated modules. Extrapallial connections are also compartmental; major extratelencephalic afferents include preglomerular nuclei (statement truncated in the catalog abstract).
ocar.future_work: How these hodological modules map onto behavioral functions is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: The roof of the adult zebrafish forebrain is divided into several neighborhoods. This tracing study, as summarized from the catalog abstract, finds those neighborhoods are only weakly wired to each other, as if they were separate workstations.
summaries.intermediate: Yáñez, Folgueira, Lamas, and Anadón (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2021) map adult zebrafish pallium with carbocyanine dyes. According to the catalog abstract, interconnectivity among pallial divisions is poor, particularly linking medial, lateral/dorsal, and posterior zones, and extrapallial afferents are similarly compartmental, with prominent preglomerular input. Summaries follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Corrales Parada, Mayer, and Chagnaud, eNeuro (2024), ‘The Dorsal Part of the Anterior Tuberal Nucleus Responds to Auditory Stimulation in Zebrafish,’ not the Yáñez et al. pallial hodology paper. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the JCN article is required for methods and figures.

plain_language_summary: The roof of the adult zebrafish forebrain is divided into several neighborhoods. This tracing study, as summarized from the catalog abstract, finds those neighborhoods are only weakly wired to each other, as if they were separate workstations.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortex and thalamus talk in both directions at massive scale; a cell-type wiring diagram of those loops is needed to interpret hierarchical cortical computation.
ocar.challenge: CTC loops are entangled with local cortical and corticocortical circuits, and inhibitory cells are embedded throughout, so a single cartoon loop is misleading.
ocar.action: Shepherd and Yamawaki, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2021), review cell-type-specific synaptic connections among major cortical and thalamic neuron types across sensory, motor, and cognitive areas.
ocar.resolution: They outline simple versus complex CTC loops, distinguish general from specialized features, and treat CTC–CC loop chains as a modular scaffold that areas modify. Inhibitory circuits are described as shaping excitatory flow. They relate findings to established CTC/CC models and to work on consciousness and perception.
ocar.future_work: They call for quantitative parameters (strengths, delays, synaptic dynamics), more species than mouse, finer subcellular targeting in connectivity matrices, and use of that knowledge in models and disease studies.

summaries.beginner: Cortex and thalamus are locked in a two-way conversation. This review sorts which cell types talk to which, and how those loops chain together across the brain.
summaries.intermediate: Shepherd and Yamawaki (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2021) synthesize cell-type-specific connectivity in cortico-thalamo-cortical loops across cortical systems. They contrast simple and complex loops, note general versus specialized motifs, and embed the loops in corticocortical hierarchies and inhibitory circuitry. The review is organizational rather than a new dataset; the conclusions ask for quantitative connection parameters and cross-species tests, with mouse remaining a core model.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a review. No new synapse counts. Consciousness/perception discussion is a pointer to ongoing work, not a solved mechanism in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Cortex and thalamus are locked in a two-way conversation. This review sorts which cell types talk to which, and how those loops chain together across the brain.

ocar.opportunity: Realistic neurons with thousands of synapses are needed to interpret micro-connectomes and to build biologically grounded networks, but full compartmental models are too slow.
ocar.challenge: Rall’s equivalent-cylinder collapse does not apply to trees with unequal lengths, conductance-based synapses, or active dendrites.
ocar.action: Amsalem, Eyal, Rogozinski, Gevaert, Kumbhar, Schürmann, and Segev, in Nature Communications (2020), introduce Neuron_Reduce, mapping synapses and active channels onto a reduced cable that preserves transfer impedance to the soma and merging equal-impedance synapses while keeping their activation times.
ocar.resolution: They report 40–250-fold faster simulations for several cell types with 10,000–100,000 synapses, while closely replicating voltage dynamics and specific dendritic computations. Thirteen morphologies are used in the methods extract, with 1,250–10,000 synapses in the accuracy tests described there. The tool is public for NEURON.
ocar.future_work: They present reduced cells as enabling unprecedented network scale, including micro-connectomic circuits and biologically inspired deep nets.

summaries.beginner: Detailed digital neurons are slow to simulate because every twig is a tiny electrical compartment. This method folds the tree into a simpler shape that still behaves like the original at the cell body, so big networks become computable.
summaries.intermediate: Amsalem et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) present Neuron_Reduce, an analytical reduction that preserves somatic transfer impedance when placing synapses and active conductances on a simplified morphology, merging synapses that share impedance. Headline speedups are 40–250× for realistic synapse counts (10,000–100,000). Methods in the extract mention 13 cell models and 50-second test simulations. Frequency parameter ω=0 gave best performance in their supplementary tests.
summaries.advanced: Open-access methods paper. Speedup range and synapse counts are the authors’ reported spans, not a single benchmark. Accuracy is relative to the parent compartmental models, not to in vivo voltages. Reduction is not a connectome.

plain_language_summary: Detailed digital neurons are slow to simulate because every twig is a tiny electrical compartment. This method folds the tree into a simpler shape that still behaves like the original at the cell body, so big networks become computable.

ocar.opportunity: Honeybee mushroom bodies are large multisensory learning centers whose synaptic microglomeruli visibly remodel with experience, offering a social-insect window onto structural plasticity.
ocar.challenge: Causal links from microglomerular change to specific behaviors remain incomplete, and work is spread across development, sensory exposure, and associative memory.
ocar.action: Groh and Rössler, in Insects (2020), review plasticity of calyx microcircuits, focusing on synapses from sensory projection neurons onto Kenyon cells, and compare honeybee results with other insects.
ocar.resolution: They synthesize evidence that differential brood care, sensory exposure, age-related hive-to-foraging transition, and associative long-term memory all associate with structural change in olfactory and visual calyx compartments, paralleled by physiological changes after learning. Mushroom bodies are framed as recoding high-dimensional sensory input into value-based codes.
ocar.future_work: The review closes on open questions about causal neuron–behavior links and colony-level sociality, and on promising integrative approaches.

summaries.beginner: A honeybee’s learning centers are packed with tiny synaptic knots that change as the bee grows up, leaves the hive, and forms memories. This review gathers what those knots look like and how they rewire.
summaries.intermediate: Groh and Rössler (Insects, 2020) review mushroom-body calyx microglomeruli in Apis. They cover projection-neuron to Kenyon-cell synapses in olfactory and visual compartments and relate structural plasticity to brood care, sensory exposure, interior–exterior transition, and associative LTM, alongside physiological retuning after learning. The honeybee is emphasized as a social-behavior model, with comparative notes to other insects. This is a review, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: Open-access review. No single synapse census for the bee MB is given in the extract. Plasticity associations are those reported in the cited literature as summarized here.

plain_language_summary: A honeybee’s learning centers are packed with tiny synaptic knots that change as the bee grows up, leaves the hive, and forms memories. This review gathers what those knots look like and how they rewire.

ocar.opportunity: If Parkinson’s Lewy pathology spreads like a trans-synaptic agent, then connectomic maps should predict where injected α-synuclein fibrils go—and where they do not.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether uptake is cell-type specific and whether connection strength sets how much pathology appears downstream.
ocar.action: Henrich, Geibl, Lakshminarasimhan, Stegmann, Giasson, Mao, Dawson, Dawson, Oertel, and Surmeier, in Science Advances (2020), inject preformed α-synuclein fibrils into mouse pedunculopontine nucleus and compare resulting pathology with anterograde and retrograde maps, including ChAT-Cre tracing of PPN cholinergics.
ocar.resolution: Within PPN, pathology is robust in Parkinson-vulnerable cholinergic neurons but not neighboring noncholinergic cells. Nearly all neurons that project to those cholinergics show pathology, yet kinetics, amount, and persistence of propagated pathology are unrelated to connection strength. Phenotype governs somatodendritic uptake; the afferent connectome restricts where pathology can go but not how severe it becomes.
ocar.future_work: They argue that connectivity plus other cellular/regional factors together explain clinical Lewy distributions and may suggest control strategies.

summaries.beginner: Parkinson’s protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, this team seeds the clumps in one brainstem region and finds that cell type decides who takes them up, while the wiring map only loosely predicts how bad the spread looks.
summaries.intermediate: Henrich et al. (Science Advances, 2020) inject α-synuclein preformed fibrils into mouse PPN and compare phospho-synuclein pathology with viral connectomic maps. Cholinergic PPN neurons, not neighbors, accumulate pathology. Afferent neurons are broadly affected, but magnitude and time course do not track coupling strength. The authors reject connection weight as the sole spreading rule. Methods in the extract include WT and ChAT-Cre mice and biotinylated fibril preparations.
summaries.advanced: Open-access. ‘Nearly all’ afferents is the paper’s wording; the extract does not give a percentage table in the selected text. Mouse PFF seeding is a model of spreading, not a human connectome. Two prior papers arguing strength-dominated spread are cited as the view they challenge.

plain_language_summary: Parkinson’s protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, this team seeds the clumps in one brainstem region and finds that cell type decides who takes them up, while the wiring map only loosely predicts how bad the spread looks.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila DIP and Dpr proteins help axons pick synaptic partners; understanding how a shared interface encodes many orthogonal specificities would explain a molecular layer of the fly connectome.
ocar.challenge: Family members are similar in sequence and structure, yet only a few of the many possible DIP–Dpr pairings bind strongly.
ocar.action: Sergeeva, Katsamba, Cosmanescu, Brewer, Ahlsen, Mannepalli, Shapiro, and Honig, in Nature Communications (2020), combine sequence, structure, energy calculations, and SPR affinity measurements across the family.
ocar.resolution: DIPs/Dprs fall into seven specificity subgroups. Binding of each subgroup is controlled by negative constraints—interface residues that block non-cognate pairs—distributed across most of the canonical interface rather than a single specificity patch. Each non-cognate subgroup pair uses a unique constraint set (steric clashes, unsatisfied charges, packing defects). They discuss this as a general evolutionary route to specificity in multi-protein families.
ocar.future_work: Implications for designing or interpreting other recognition families are conceptual; switching specificity in tests required altering at least three constraints in cases they examined.

summaries.beginner: Fly neurons use families of look-alike surface proteins to choose partners. This paper shows that what often matters is not a special ‘on’ switch but many small ‘don’t bind them’ features scattered over the same handshake surface.
summaries.intermediate: Sergeeva et al. (Nature Communications, 2020) partition Drosophila DIP and Dpr proteins into seven SPR-defined specificity subgroups. Homology models, FoldX, and binding measurements indicate that orthogonal pairing is enforced by negative constraints covering most of the shared Ig interface. Physical origins include charge repulsion, buried unsatisfied charges, and hydrophobic packing defects. Intra-subgroup affinities in the extract are generally described as in the 10 μM range. The work is structural/biophysical, not a circuit reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Open-access. Seven subgroups and the 10 μM KD remark are the authors’. Catalog pipeline tags include segmentation; this paper is protein biochemistry of recognition molecules used in neuronal targeting.

plain_language_summary: Fly neurons use families of look-alike surface proteins to choose partners. This paper shows that what often matters is not a special ‘on’ switch but many small ‘don’t bind them’ features scattered over the same handshake surface.

ocar.opportunity: Memories can last while synapses and which cells fire for a memory turn over; a circuit mechanism that keeps representations consistent without a teacher would reconcile plasticity with persistence.
ocar.challenge: Standard assembly models assume a stable neuron set, yet experiments show spontaneous synaptic change and drifting codes, including in long-term memory areas.
ocar.action: Kossio, Goedeke, Klos, and Memmesheimer, in a September 2020 bioRxiv preprint (catalog venue PNAS), simulate assemblies that exchange neurons because of synaptic turnover and noisy spiking, with STDP plus homeostasis compensating without teaching signals.
ocar.resolution: Assemblies drift completely—no preserved core—yet representational structure, inputs, and outputs stay consistent, supporting persistent memory and simple computations. Interior neurons switch which memory they join; periphery neurons are more stable. The model is used to explain evolving fear-memory representations.
ocar.future_work: They argue memory systems must be understood as complete input–assembly–output loops because parts constantly change.

summaries.beginner: We often picture a memory as a fixed club of neurons. This theory paper says the club’s membership can turn over completely, while unsupervised plasticity keeps the memory itself intact.
summaries.intermediate: Kossio, Goedeke, Klos, and Memmesheimer (bioRxiv 2020; catalog lists PNAS) propose drifting assemblies: spontaneous remodeling and irregular spiking exchange neurons, while STDP and homeostasis keep assemblies aligned with inputs and readouts without external error. There is no stable core connectivity or invariant cell set. They contrast this with models that preserve a core, retrain, or use feedback, and they link the idea to changing fear-memory engrams. The extract is the preprint text.
summaries.advanced: Preprint extract of work catalogued as PNAS; treat bibliographic venue as the catalog record and the PDF as the bioRxiv version. No new experimental connectome. Drift and compensation are simulation results.

plain_language_summary: We often picture a memory as a fixed club of neurons. This theory paper says the club’s membership can turn over completely, while unsupervised plasticity keeps the memory itself intact.

ocar.opportunity: If cortex is built from a repeated canonical circuit, systematic regional gradients in excitation and inhibition could explain how areas acquire qualitatively different functions.
ocar.challenge: Slice physiology has been dominated by sensory cortex, so differences along the hierarchy have been under-documented and treated as noise.
ocar.action: Wang, in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2020), reviews experimental and theoretical evidence that synaptic excitation and inhibition vary as macroscopic gradients across neocortex and that those gradients are abnormal in mental illness.
ocar.resolution: Quantitative gradient differences can yield qualitatively new dynamics via bifurcation. He reports an increasing excitation gradient along hierarchy (spine counts, NMDAR-related gene expression) and a shift in inhibition toward more input-controlling SST+/CB+ versus output-controlling PV+ interneurons in higher areas. Gene-expression variation is described as low-dimensional and aligned with T1w/T2w hierarchy.
ocar.future_work: He notes that a multi-area NMDAR excitation gradient still needs direct elucidation, that PV/pyramidal ratios and SST subtypes need fuller mapping, and that gene expression is only an indirect link to function.

summaries.beginner: Every patch of cortex looks a bit like every other, yet they do different jobs. This review argues that excitation and inhibition change smoothly from sensory areas to association areas, and those slopes can flip circuits into new kinds of behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Xiao-Jing Wang (Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2020) reviews macroscopic gradients of cortical excitation and inhibition. Canonical minicolumns are the starting motif; area differences are treated as structured, not random. Headline claims in the concluding section are a hierarchy-aligned increase in recurrent/NMDA-related excitation and a rising SST+/CB+ to PV+ inhibitory ratio. Bifurcation is the mathematical bridge from quantitative slopes to qualitative function. Psychiatric disruption of the gradients is discussed.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a review. Gradient evidence is synthesized from cited studies; this paper does not report a new connectome. NMDAR gradient ‘remains to be elucidated’ is the author’s own caveat.

plain_language_summary: Every patch of cortex looks a bit like every other, yet they do different jobs. This review argues that excitation and inhibition change smoothly from sensory areas to association areas, and those slopes can flip circuits into new kinds of behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical neurons integrate synapses over millimeters and two hemispheres; activity imaging that is both mesoscale and spine-resolving would link dendrites to large circuits in awake mice.
ocar.challenge: Point-scanning two-photon imaging that is fast enough for volumes usually sacrifices either field of view or synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Lu, Liang, Meng, Zhou, Svoboda, Paninski, and Ji, in Nature Methods (2020), add a Bessel-beam module to a two-photon mesoscope and perform calcium imaging in awake mice.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate volumetric activity imaging with synaptic resolution over mesoscale fields, including entire dendritic arbors and ensembles in multiple cortical areas across both hemispheres. A density bound in the methods discussion illustrates when Bessel projection remains unambiguous (example: 25,000 somata/mm³ upper bound under stated GCaMP6s assumptions versus 3,402 GABAergic neurons/mm³ in their Fig. 3). Thorlabs licensed related IP from HHMI.
ocar.future_work: Labeling density, sensor kinetics, and Bessel length jointly limit separable structures; the paper is a methods demonstration, not an all-cortex functional connectome.

summaries.beginner: Watching synapses fire across a wide stretch of mouse cortex is usually a choice between zooming in or seeing the big picture. This team shapes the laser into a long thin focus so they can do both, even across two hemispheres.
summaries.intermediate: Lu, Liang, Meng, Zhou, Svoboda, Paninski, and Ji (Nature Methods, 2020) insert a Bessel focus module into a two-photon mesoscope for rapid volumetric calcium imaging at synaptic resolution in awake mice. Applications include full dendritic spans and multi-area, bi-hemispheric ensembles. Automatic ROI detection uses CNMF-E-style code. A labeling-density inequality in the extract sets when only one active structure occupies the projected volume. Mesoscope and Bessel IP were licensed to Thorlabs.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript of a brief methods paper. Density numbers are hypothetical bounds and one reported GABAergic density, not a cortex-wide census. Synaptic resolution refers to optical spines/synapses in fluorescence, not EM.

plain_language_summary: Watching synapses fire across a wide stretch of mouse cortex is usually a choice between zooming in or seeing the big picture. This team shapes the laser into a long thin focus so they can do both, even across two hemispheres.

ocar.opportunity: Counting and classifying central synapses across mesoscale volumes in animals and archived human tissue would show how injury and neurodegeneration disconnect circuits.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and densely packed; many super-resolution workflows are slow, specialized, or require large section arrays.
ocar.action: Sauerbeck, Gangolli, Reitz, Salyards, Kim, Hemingway, Gratuze, Makkapati, Kerschensteiner, Holtzman, Brody, and Kummer, in Neuron (2020), introduce SEQUIN, a super-resolution imaging and analysis workflow for synapse quantification and nanostructural/molecular characterization.
ocar.resolution: SEQUIN identifies delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse traumatic brain injury. Similar loss appears in three murine Alzheimer-related models, where mesoscale mapping shows regional synaptic vulnerability. The method uses standard histology and exogenous labels, enabling human tissue and archived samples. It does not measure physiology directly but can quantify nanostructural correlates of strength (separation, size).
ocar.future_work: They compare SEQUIN’s niche with EM, array tomography, and STED/SMLM, and suggest pairing with activity reporters such as SynaptoZip or SynTagMA.

summaries.beginner: Synapses are tiny and packed like sand, so counting them in a chunk of brain is hard. This paper offers a practical super-resolution recipe and uses it to show that diffuse head injury, like some Alzheimer models, quietly deletes cortical connections.
summaries.intermediate: Sauerbeck et al. (Neuron, 2020) present SEQUIN for rapid super-resolution synapse counts in animal and human tissue without large histological arrays. They report delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse TBI and comparable loss with regional vulnerability in three mouse Alzheimer-related models. Discussion places SEQUIN as accessible and artifact-resistant relative to more specialized modalities; EM remains superior for ultrastructure, array tomography for multiplexing. Holtzman disclosures are listed in the extract.
summaries.advanced: PMC author manuscript. The extract’s summary does not give a single percent-loss figure. ‘Three murine models’ is the paper’s phrasing. SEQUIN infers synapses from labeled puncta geometry, not from EM.

plain_language_summary: Synapses are tiny and packed like sand, so counting them in a chunk of brain is hard. This paper offers a practical super-resolution recipe and uses it to show that diffuse head injury, like some Alzheimer models, quietly deletes cortical connections.

ocar.opportunity: Sex differences in synapse maps of shared neuron classes would show how the same connectome template is edited for sex-specific behavior.
ocar.challenge: How a conserved DMRT transcription factor could act only in one sex in shared neurons was unknown.
ocar.action: Bayer, Stecky, Neal, Katsamba, Ahlsen, Balaji, Hoppe, Shapiro, Oren-Suissa, and Hobert, in eLife (2020), study C. elegans dmd-4 in sex-shared phasmid sensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: dmd-4 is expressed in two phasmid classes in hermaphrodites, not males, and promotes hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connectivity and function. Sex specificity is posttranslational: ubiquitin binding to the conserved DMA domain stabilizes the protein in a sex-specific way. A human DMRT homolog is reported to be controlled similarly, suggesting broader relevance.
ocar.future_work: The discussion places DMRTs as a rare shared sexual-differentiation family across animals and contrasts dmd-4’s ubiquitin/DMA logic with transcriptional sex-specificity of other worm DMRTs such as mab-3 and dmd-3.

summaries.beginner: Male and female worms share many of the same neurons but wire some of them differently. This paper finds a switch protein that is kept stable only in hermaphrodites, and that stability is enough to build the female-like connections.
summaries.intermediate: Bayer et al. (eLife, 2020) show that the DMRT gene dmd-4 is expressed in two classes of sex-shared C. elegans phasmid neurons in hermaphrodites only, where it supports sex-specific synapses and function. Regulation is via sex-specific protein stability through ubiquitin engagement of the DMA domain, not solely transcriptional on/off. They report analogous control of a human DMRT homolog. The study links molecular sex determination to dimorphic connectivity in an otherwise shared nervous system.
summaries.advanced: Open-access. ‘Two classes’ of phasmid neurons are those named in the abstract; the selected text does not list synapse-by-synapse rewiring counts from White/Cook connectomes. Human homolog claim is the authors’ experimental extension, not a human-circuit map.

plain_language_summary: Male and female worms share many of the same neurons but wire some of them differently. This paper finds a switch protein that is kept stable only in hermaphrodites, and that stability is enough to build the female-like connections.

ocar.opportunity: Relating spike-train correlations to synaptic wiring is central to interpreting population recordings and connectomes together.
ocar.challenge: Balanced-network theory of the asynchronous state assumed uncorrelated feedforward input; real upstream spike trains are often correlated.
ocar.action: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum, in Physical Review E (2019), as described in the catalog abstract, analyze balanced networks that receive correlated feedforward spike trains.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports that correlated feedforward input produces much larger downstream correlations than the classical asynchronous state, yielding a ‘correlated state’ with tight excitatory–inhibitory balance consistent with in vivo cortex. Earlier work is summarized as showing very weak average correlations that can still hide some strong pairs when feedforward input is uncorrelated.
ocar.future_work: Extensions beyond the abstract’s scope are not specified here.

summaries.beginner: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper, summarized from the catalog abstract, says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.
summaries.intermediate: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum (Physical Review E, 2019) study balanced networks with correlated feedforward input. According to the catalog abstract, that input drives a correlated state with larger spike-train correlations and a tight E–I balance matching in vivo observations, unlike the weakly correlated asynchronous state obtained with uncorrelated feedforward spikes. Summaries follow that abstract because the associated PDF is a known mismatch.
summaries.advanced: pdf_trust is mismatch: the on-disk PDF is not Baker et al. 2019 (extract pipeline flags this work_id as Keijser and Sadeh 2026). The supplied text is the catalog abstract only. Independent reading of the Physical Review E paper is required for equations, figures, and parameters.

plain_language_summary: Brain models often assume incoming spike trains are independent, which keeps cortical cells nearly uncorrelated. This theory paper, summarized from the catalog abstract, says that if those inputs are themselves correlated, the whole network enters a much more correlated state.

ocar.opportunity: Lipid membranes define organelles and neurites, but expansion microscopy had lacked a validated lipid tag, limiting optical nanoscale views of membranes relevant to connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Standard ExM visualizes proteins and nucleic acids; lipids need a gel-anchorable stain, and protease digestion destroys epitopes needed for protein–lipid overlays.
ocar.action: Karagiannis, Kang, Shin, Emenari, Asano, Lin, Costa, Marblestone, Kasthuri, and Boyden, in a November 2019 bioRxiv preprint, introduce a chemical membrane tag and membrane expansion microscopy (mExM) with post-expansion antibody labeling after heat/detergent homogenization instead of proteinase K.
ocar.resolution: They image protein–lipid relationships in ER (calnexin), Golgi (giantin), mitochondria (Tom20), nuclear envelope (NUP98), and myelin (MBP), with lipid and antibody signals colocalized. The protocol is proposed for cell–cell interactions, intracellular transport, and neural connectomics. Expansion after antibody buffer is about 2× before full ~4.5× water expansion.
ocar.future_work: Utility for connectomics is prospective; the extract focuses on organelle membranes and myelin rather than a dense synaptic map.

summaries.beginner: Expansion microscopy usually lights up proteins or DNA, not the fatty membranes of cells. This preprint adds a membrane stain and a gentler expansion recipe so lipids and proteins can be seen together at nanoscale with a light microscope.
summaries.intermediate: Karagiannis, Kang, and colleagues (bioRxiv, 2019) describe mExM: a lipid-optimized expansion protocol using a gel-compatible membrane tag (pGk5b in the extract) and post-expansion antibodies after SDS/DTT heat homogenization rather than proteinase K. They show colocalization with organelle membrane proteins (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, nuclear membrane) and myelin basic protein. Linear expansion is the usual ExM ~4.5× after water, with ~2× in antibody buffer. Kasthuri and Boyden are among the authors; connectomic use is listed as a motivation.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. Organelle examples are those named in the extract. This is optical expansion imaging, not EM. Connectomics application is proposed, not demonstrated as a full wiring diagram.

plain_language_summary: Expansion microscopy usually lights up proteins or DNA, not the fatty membranes of cells. This preprint adds a membrane stain and a gentler expansion recipe so lipids and proteins can be seen together at nanoscale with a light microscope.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical microconnectomes contain both pairwise (first-order) statistics and higher-order motifs such as cliques; isolating their dynamical effects would show what morphological diversity buys a circuit.
ocar.challenge: First- and higher-order structure usually covary, so their impact on activity is confounded.
ocar.action: Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann, in Network Neuroscience (2020; catalog year 2019), compare the Blue Brain NMC microcircuit with a ‘cloud-model’ control that keeps first-order connectivity (including distance dependence and m-type strengths) but derives excitatory connections from average morphologies, reducing common-neighbor bias.
ocar.resolution: Morphological diversity within types yields more heterogeneous degrees, more directed cliques, small-world topology, and hub neurons—features weakened in the cloud-model. Spontaneous and evoked dynamics look similar at first glance, but spike counts follow in-degree, population responses become more excitatory and less reliable, and the hierarchical dependence of pairwise correlations on clique position is weaker without higher-order structure.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that models matched on first-order statistics can still differ drastically in higher-order structure and in nuanced activity statistics.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is more than who connects to whom on average; clumps of all-to-all connected cells also matter. This modelling study keeps the simple connection rules the same but removes those clumps, and some firing patterns change.
summaries.intermediate: Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann (Network Neuroscience, 2020) contrast the neocortical microcircuit (NMC) model with a cloud-model that preserves pairwise connection statistics while flattening morphological diversity. Higher-order features (cliques, hubs, small-worldness, heterogeneous degrees) drop in the control. Average activity remains similar, but correlation structure tied to directed simplices weakens. The study is in silico on reconstructed morphologies, not a new EM volume.
summaries.advanced: Published Network Neuroscience article (DOI netn_a_00124); catalog lists bioRxiv/2019. ‘Drastically different higher-order structure’ is the authors’ phrasing. No new experimental recordings.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is more than who connects to whom on average; clumps of all-to-all connected cells also matter. This modelling study keeps the simple connection rules the same but removes those clumps, and some firing patterns change.

ocar.opportunity: A classified human brain connectome that combines anatomy with neurophysiology would help relate structure to function and to clinical mapping.
ocar.challenge: Many connectivity methods exist across EEG/MEG stimulation, imaging, and graph theory, and they are not automatically commensurate.
ocar.action: Rossini, Di Iorio, Bentivoglio, Bertini, Ferreri, Gerloff, Ilmoniemi, Miraglia, Nitsche, Pestilli, Rosanova, Shirota, Tesoriero, Ugawa, Vecchio, Ziemann, and Hallett, in Clinical Neurophysiology (2019), as described in the catalog abstract, review IFCN-relevant methods for studying the human connectome with emphasis on neurophysiological techniques.
ocar.resolution: The abstract describes a multimodality program to identify networks with neurobiologically meaningful, computable measures, integrating neurophysiology with flow/metabolic neuroimaging so that anatomical and functional connections can be placed on one map for structure–function and clinical interpretation.
ocar.future_work: Specific method-by-method recommendations beyond the abstract are not taken from the mismatched PDF.

summaries.beginner: Doctors and scientists map human brain networks with electrical recordings, magnetic stimulation, and scanners. This IFCN review, summarized from the catalog abstract, surveys those tools and how to combine them.
summaries.intermediate: Rossini and colleagues (Clinical Neurophysiology, 2019) review methods for the human connectome with a neurophysiology focus, in an IFCN-sponsored paper. According to the catalog abstract, the aim is to classify networks with computable measures and to integrate physiological mapping with neuroimaging of flow and metabolism. Summaries follow that abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Karimi, Li, Taymourtash, Jaimes, Grant, and Warfield, bioRxiv (2025), ‘Charting the Normal Development of Structural Brain Connectivity in Utero using Diffusion MRI,’ analyzing 198 fetuses from dHCP—not the 2019 IFCN methods review. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Clinical Neurophysiology paper is required.
